units.translation: never; in the manuscripts it is found written either as one word or separately as οὔ ποτε [never], never at all, just as μήποτε [never] or μή ποτε [never] is written, about which I have spoken in the Lexicon Sophocleum p. 299. And not rarely other words are placed between μή [not] or οὐ [not] and ποτέ [ever], about which will be said under the entry ποτέ [ever].
never shall the counsels of mortal men transgress the harmony of Zeus
never does he care for this man's heralds' messages
but those who never hoped reaped well
as to those who never hoped to have this favor
for this house the chorus never leaves
never abandoning the thought of toil
but utterly destroyed he could never become
never will you find a drink
as much as from others you could never have of mortals
οὐ πω [not yet], with other words interposed.
he does not yet know how to be prudent
and no one has ever seen Zeus defeated
such a one as Persia never yet covered
by the contrivances of Zeus, not yet willing to destroy the race
and not yet is the blood of the gods faded for them
never yet did a day without hunting send Actaeon
for the one who will give relief has not yet been born
never yet did I see such a clear sign
never yet did I endure such a calamity
not yet do you boast this word over him as he lies
I have not yet cried out the noble song

The second gloss is also in Hesychius and in Bachmann's Anecdota vol. 1, p. 322, 19, where it is corruptly written οὐράνιζεν · τὸ πρὸς [reached the sky: the ...] etc. But with this verb must be compared the verb προσαιθρίζειν [to expose to the open air], which I restored to Aeschylus Agam. v. 301. A third verb of this kind Hesychius noted, προσ-αυρίζουσα χερσαίᾳ τροχῇ: ὑπὸ τῆς αὔρας ή νοτὶς προσπίπτουσα τῇ τροχῇ. δύναται δὲ οἷον καταλαμβάνουσα · ἐπαυρεῖν γὰρ τὸ καταλαμβάνειν καὶ ἐπιτυγχάνειν [touching upon the dry wheel: the moisture falling upon the wheel by the breeze. It can mean, as it were, seizing; for ἐπαυρεῖν means to seize and to hit upon]. In these words it is easy to recognize this verse of Aeschylus, unless I am mistaken, νοτὶς προσαυρίζουσα χερσαίᾳ τροχῇ [the moisture touching upon the dry wheel].
let it reach the sky: let it go up to heaven
it reached the sky: it goes up to heaven
to expose to the open air
touching upon the dry wheel: the moisture falling upon the wheel by the breeze. It can mean, as it were, seizing; for ἐπαυρεῖν means to seize and to hit upon
the moisture touching upon the dry wheel
Of calamity arising from the gods
the paths of the heavenly stars
of the gods, both heavenly and of the marketplace
heavenly songs of supplication to the gods
a whirlwind lifting a thunderbolt, a heavenly grief
a torch reaching to heaven rises
conquering heaven or the heavenly ones.
and I lament the ruin of my wife, conquering heaven
the Titans, children of Uranus and Earth
